head:
Profile · 75 and over

At 75 and over: getting stronger, keeping your balance and not being afraid to move

You are 75 or older, or you are reading this article for a parent, a partner or a friend. This article follows one question: at this age, and even with chronic illness, does exercise make a difference, where do you start without getting hurt, and how do you keep going? It ends with a plan in phases. It is an editorial proposal, not a prescription: it does not replace your doctor or a professional in adapted physical activity.

The question

A typical profile, to fix ideas. This character is illustrative and does not correspond to any real person. A woman of 82 lives alone in an apartment with a staircase. She has high blood pressure and osteoarthritis, and takes several medications. A year ago she fell in the bathroom, without serious injury. Since then she goes out less, avoids the stairs, and gets up from her armchair carefully. Her daughter, who phones her every evening, wonders whether she should push her to walk or, on the contrary, ask her to stop taking risks.

This situation raises two problems that feed each other. The first is physical: leg muscles, balance and walking speed decline, often without anyone noticing. The second is psychological: the fear of falling again leads to moving less, which makes things even more fragile.

The question

After 75, with frailty, chronic illness or a fear of falling, can a measurable exercise programme really improve strength, balance and the risk of falls, and how do you start it safely and keep it up over time?

We answer in six steps: what frailty is, what research says about very old people, what works for falls, what is known about the fear of falling, what you need to know about protein, and then what makes people keep going. The action plan comes afterwards.

What is at stake

After 75, the goal is not performance. It is staying able to get up, walk outdoors, wash and get home, without depending on someone. The article “Staying independent after 65: strength, balance, falls” in this series shows that the risk of falls soars between 65 and 85: at 85 and over, the hospitalisation rate after a fall is about nine times that of 65-74-year-olds, and the death rate about twenty-nine times (figures reported by Santé publique France). A fall is not only a broken bone: it is often the start of a cycle in which you go out less and lose even more strength.

There is also a question of choice: sparing yourself passes for prudence, but if exercise is effective and safe, it has a cost. And there is a stake for the carer: helping without deciding in the other person's place.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · The framework

Frailty is not age: it can be spotted, and it can be worked on

In geriatrics, “frail” has a definition. Linda Fried and her colleagues set it out in 2001 from the Cardiovascular Health Study, which followed 5,317 adults aged 65 and over. A person is called frail when they meet at least three of five criteria: unintentional weight loss, self-reported exhaustion, low grip strength, slow walking, low physical activity.1,2 With one or two criteria, it is called pre-frailty.

Frailty can be counted: three criteria out of five or more

Definition of the Fried phenotype (at least 3 criteria out of 5: frail; 1 or 2: intermediate). Only weight loss has a threshold that was read (at least 10 pounds, about 4.5 kg, in a year); the other thresholds are not reproduced here. Bar heights: illustration, not data. Sources: Fried 2001; Today's Geriatric Medicine.1,2

In this cohort, 6.9% of people were frail, and the proportion rose with age. Over three years, frailty predicted falls, worsening mobility, hospitalisation and death, with risk ratios of 1.82 to 4.46 before adjustment and 1.29 to 2.24 after adjustment for other factors.1

What this means

Frailty is not an end-of-the-road diagnosis. It is a risk label, with an intermediate stage where you can act. A pre-frail person in this study was more likely to become frail (odds ratio of 2.63 after adjustment): that is the argument for looking early.

A related term, sarcopenia, refers to the loss of muscle strength and mass. The European consensus EWGSOP2 describes it as a muscle disease, and makes muscle weakness a central criterion: a muscle that produces little force already raises suspicion of the diagnosis, low muscle mass confirms it, and poor physical performance points to a severe form.3 According to a study that uses these thresholds, sarcopenia is called probable below 27 kg of grip strength in men or 16 kg in women, or when five chair stands take more than 15 seconds.4 This last test can be done at home, with someone next to you: we come back to it in the plan. Frailty and sarcopenia overlap: in both, leg strength is at the heart of the problem (editorial reading).

The next question is therefore whether leg strength can be restored at an age when people believe “it is too late”.

Step 2 of 6 · What is possible

Even at 90, muscles respond to training

The historic work is that of Maria Fiatarone. In 1990, in JAMA, her team had ten frail volunteers living in an institution, aged 90 on average, do eight weeks of high-intensity strength training. Nine completed it. Their strength rose by 174% on average, tandem walking speed by 48%, and thigh muscle area by 9%.5 This first result is spectacular, but it rests on only nine volunteers, and the abstract read does not mention a control group.

She therefore repeated it on a larger scale. In 1994, in the New England Journal of Medicine, a randomised trial followed 100 frail nursing-home residents, aged 87.1 on average (from 72 to 98), for ten weeks. They were split into four groups: exercise, nutritional supplement, both, or neither. Strength rose by 113% in those who trained, against 3% in the others. Walking speed gained 11.8% against a drop of 1.0%, and stair-climbing power 28.4% against 3.6%. The nutritional supplement alone had no effect on these primary outcomes; 94% of participants completed the trial.6

Trained in strength at 87-90, frail residents gained in strength and walking

Means from the two Fiatarone trials. 1990: 9 people aged 90 on average, 8 weeks, no control group in the abstract read. 1994: 100 people aged 87 on average, 10 weeks, randomised. The strength percentages cannot be compared from one trial to the other (different tests and loads). Sources: Fiatarone 1990; Fiatarone 1994 (abstracts).5,6

What this means

A 90-year-old muscle still responds to load. A gain of 113% does not mean “twice as strong at everything”: strength is measured on one specific movement, at a low starting load. The walking gain is the most telling for daily life. Also keep in mind an uncomfortable fact: the nutritional supplement alone changed nothing. The lever is movement.

These results come from volunteer residents in a supervised setting: that is not the same as training alone at home. What do the trials as a whole show?

Step 3 of 6 · Multicomponent programmes

Strength, balance and walking together give the most consistent results

In 2013, Cadore and colleagues summarised the randomised trials of supervised exercise in frail older people: 20 trials, including 10 of multicomponent programmes (strength, endurance, balance), 6 of strength training, 3 of balance (tai chi) and 1 of endurance.7,8 The results: leg strength improves in 9 trials out of 13, falls decrease in 7 trials out of 10, balance improves in 7 out of 10 and walking in 6 out of 11.7

In most trials, exercise improves strength, balance and falls in frail people

Number of trials in which the trained group did better than the control group, out of the number of trials that measured each outcome. Source: Cadore et al., Rejuvenation Research, 2013, read on the PMC copy.7

What this means

The result is not unanimous: one trial in three to one in two, depending on the outcome, showed no benefit. The authors attribute part of these failures to programmes that were too low in intensity, done at home, or centred on sociability rather than effort.7 A programme without effort does not give the same results; but the quality of the trials was uneven and the authors call for confirmation.

The authors propose as a prescription, to be confirmed: 2 to 3 strength sessions a week, 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, starting at 20 to 30% of the maximum load and progressing up to about 80%, with functional movements such as getting up from a chair; endurance by walking, from 5-10 minutes to 15-30 minutes, at an effort of 12 to 14 on the Borg scale (“somewhat hard”); and balance, from easiest to hardest (feet together, tandem, standing on one foot).7 Few adverse effects are reported (one shoulder pain, one withdrawal for medical reasons), in trials supervised by professionals.7

In very old hospitalised people, in a Spanish randomised trial of 370 patients aged 75 and over (87.3 on average), a programme inspired by Vivifrail, lasting 5 to 7 days (5 days median), with two 20-minute sessions a day, improved the SPPB physical performance score by 2.2 points compared with usual care (confidence interval 1.7 to 2.6), and independence in daily activities (Barthel index) by 6.9 points. No adverse event was attributed to the programme. But length of stay, in-hospital falls, readmission at 3 months and mortality did not change.9

A change of 0.54 points in the SPPB is seen as small and 1.34 as substantial: the observed difference exceeds this latter threshold (editorial comparison).17 Vivifrail is a multicomponent programme that classifies people according to their SPPB (levels A, B+, C, C+, D in a Mexican trial). This 12-week, non-randomised trial in 61 women aged 65 to 80 (at least 3 sessions of 45 to 60 minutes a week) saw the share of participants at risk of falling go from 70% to 12.5%, against 52.4% to 63.6% in the control group. The study is small and non-randomised.10,11

That leaves falling, which is what people fear most.

Step 4 of 6 · Falls

Programmes that work on balance reduce falls

The reference is the Cochrane review by Sherrington and colleagues (2019): 108 randomised trials, 23,407 people living at home, 76 years old on average, 77% women. With all types of exercise combined, the rate of falls drops by about 23% with a high level of evidence, or about 195 fewer falls per 1,000 people followed for a year, if the control group had 850.12

Working on balance reduces falls, especially when combined with strengthening

Reduction in the fall rate by type of exercise, with the review's level of certainty. Walking alone, strengthening alone and dance: insufficient evidence to conclude. Source: Cochrane, Sherrington et al., 2019 (plain-language summary).12

What this means

A programme that combines several types of exercise, especially balance and strengthening, is the one that reduces falls the most: about a third fewer falls. The trials do not allow us to say whether walking alone reduces falls: it remains useful, but it is not what protects best.

Effects on fall-related fractures (about 27% fewer) and on falls requiring medical care (about 39% fewer) exist, with low certainty. Effects on falls leading to hospital are uncertain. Adverse events, mostly muscular and minor, are poorly reported.12 The summary read says nothing about frail people or nursing homes: the figures apply to people living at home.

One specific programme has been tested many times: the Otago programme, developed in New Zealand. It combines leg strengthening with ankle weights of about 1 kg at the start, balance exercises of increasing difficulty, about 30 minutes three times a week, and walking for up to 30 minutes at least twice a week, with a few home visits by a trained professional. In the trials cited by a presentation document, it reduced falls by 32% in women aged 80 and over in one trial, and by 35% when four trials were pooled.19 Figures from a presentation document, not from the original articles (see also the article “Staying independent after 65: strength, balance, falls”).

That leaves the mind of the person who has fallen, or who fears doing so.

Step 5 of 6 · The fear of falling

The fear of falling leads to moving less, and exercise may reduce it

In the British CARE75+ cohort, 543 people aged 75 and over (80.3 on average) who did not limit their activities at the start were followed for a year. For 10.1% of them (55 people), the fear of falling led to restricting their activities. Those with more frailty (odds ratio 1.58), who had fallen during the year (2.22) or whose Timed Up and Go test was slower (1.08 per unit) were more likely to restrict themselves.14,15

What this means

The fear does not come from nowhere: it follows frailty, a fall already experienced and reduced mobility, which makes it reasonable. But it has a cost: the less you move, the less you keep the strength that protects. It is a cycle, but these are associations: the study does not say that reducing the fear reduces the restrictions.

What can be done with this fear? The Cochrane review by Kendrick (2014) pooled 30 studies, 2,878 people living at home, aged 65 and over. Exercise slightly reduces the fear of falling just after the programme (24 studies, 1,692 people; low certainty), but at 6 months and beyond the results are small and uncertain (very low certainty). Exercise did not increase falls.13

What this means

Solid: exercise does not make you fall more. Uncertain: in the long term, the fear does not necessarily go away. This argues for gently resuming the feared movements (getting up, turning round, stepping up), with a support within reach, and for measuring visible progress without waiting for the fear to fade (editorial proposal).

That leaves nutrition.

Step 6 of 6 · Protein

Protein supports muscle, without promising miracles

The PROT-AGE expert group recommends, for healthy adults over 65, an intake of at least 1.0 to 1.2 g of protein per kilo of body weight per day; at least 1.2 g/kg/day for those who exercise; and 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day in acute or chronic illness. The exception: in severe kidney disease (filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²) outside dialysis, it may be necessary to restrict it.20 The MSD Manual states that the optimal intake is unknown, and also cites 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/day for people without chronic kidney disease.21

To give an order of magnitude, derived calculation: at 70 kg, 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg corresponds to 70 to 84 g of protein per day, from all sources combined. This is not individual advice. It depends on kidney function, illnesses and treatments, and belongs with your doctor or a dietitian. And remember the Fiatarone trial: the supplement alone did not change strength.6 Timing of meals, protein quality and supplements: the experts judge the evidence insufficient for precise recommendations.20 The French National Authority for Health (HAS) sheet on falls recommends correcting nutritional deficits and considering vitamin D for people confined to their home or to an institution (2005 sheet).22

Why, then, do many people not start or stop?

The real obstacles, and how to remove them

Obstacle 1: “It is too late.” The trials above included people aged 87 to 90. This does not guarantee the same result for you, but the belief is not supported by these data.

Obstacle 2: fear, in the patient and in those close to them. Exercise did not increase falls in Kendrick's review.13 For the carer: suggest rather than impose. The HAS sheet asks that each proposal be explained and negotiated, taking into account the person's fears and values.22 Staying beside them without doing it in their place: editorial advice, not a trial result.

Obstacle 3: being alone. A review of 21 trials (5,275 people) on preventing frailty found that group exercise delayed or reduced frailty, whereas individual one-to-one exercise showed no effectiveness (effects not quantified in the abstract read; authors not read).28 If you can, look for a supervised group session (adapted physical activity); your doctor can point you towards one.

Obstacle 4: the system, not willpower. A habit is built. In Lally's study, 96 volunteers, students aged 27 on average, followed a new daily behaviour: the time for it to become automatic was 66 days median for the 39 people whose curve could be used, with a range of 18 to 254 days. A missed day hardly mattered.25 A study on young people: keep the order of magnitude (weeks to months) and the fact that one missed day erases nothing. “Implementation intentions”, that is, sentences of the type “when X happens, I do Y” (“after my coffee, I do my chair stands”), have a mean effect of d = 0.65 on goal attainment (meta-analysis of 94 tests, read on a secondary page; a 2024 update gives 0.27 to 0.66).26 Finally, a meta-regression of 122 evaluations (44,747 participants) found that self-monitoring, combined with at least one other control technique (setting a goal, comparing with the goal), gave an effect of 0.42 against 0.26 for other interventions.27 Hence the session log in the plan.

What this means

The plan is the same for everyone, basically: a little strength, balance and walking, often, progressing slowly. What changes at 75 and over is the starting point (seated), the dose (short), the precautions (medical advice, support, someone nearby) and the obstacles (fear, loneliness, pain). The hardest part is not knowing what to do, it is doing it again tomorrow.

The action plan in phases

Here is a 12-week trajectory followed by maintenance. It is an editorial proposal, built from the doses of the programmes studied (Cadore, Otago, LIFE): it has not been tested as it stands. It does not replace a professional's advice.

Before the first week: advice, place, measurements

  • Ask for medical advice.The PAR-Q+ questionnaire directs you to a professional as soon as any answer to the health questions is positive.23 The advice of the American Academy of Family Physicians is more flexible: most older people can exercise safely, and advice is needed if in doubt or if there is poorly controlled illness.24 At 75 and over, with chronic illness, multiple medications or a recent fall, the editors recommend systematic advice: this is a choice of prudence, not a sourced obligation. The HAS also asks for a consultation after a fall and a medication review.22
  • Prepare the place.A stable chair against a wall, a worktop or a solid chair back to lean on, closed shoes, a clear room, a phone within reach, and if possible a person nearby (editorial proposal).
  • Do the three measurements, once.Chair stand: the time for five stands (more than 15 seconds is a probable sarcopenia threshold).4 Walking speed: 4 metres at your usual pace, speed equals 4 divided by the time in seconds; 5.0 s gives 0.8 m/s, a “median” survival benchmark for age.16 Balance: hold feet together, then one foot slightly in front of the other, then tandem, for up to 10 seconds each, as in the SPPB.17 Note the three values in a notebook. For how to do each test and how to read the thresholds by age, see the article “Staying independent after 65: strength, balance, falls”. If you are afraid of falling during a test, do not do it alone.

The plan rises from 60 to 150 minutes a week over twelve weeks

Editorial proposal, not tested as it stands. Heights: 3 sessions of 15, 25, 30, 30 minutes of strength-balance, plus 3 outings of 5, 10, 15 minutes then 2 outings of 30 minutes. The 150-minute line is derived from the description of the Otago programme (30 min three times, walking 30 min twice). Dose sources: Cadore 2013; Otago.7,19

Weeks 1 to 4: set up the habit (about 60 minutes a week)

Three sessions of 15 minutes, three outings or walks of 5 minutes during the day, always at the same time. Example of a session: five to eight chair stands, with your arms if needed, aiming to do them without; stand with feet together then one foot slightly in front of the other with a hand on a support; rise onto your toes holding the worktop. The level of effort: you can talk without being out of breath, at "somewhat hard" at most (12 to 14 on the Borg scale in the Cadore review).7,24 Do not try to progress: try not to miss a single session. Choose a precise trigger (“after the 9 o'clock coffee”) and tick off each session in your notebook.

Weeks 5 to 8: add load (about 105 minutes a week)

Three sessions of 25 minutes, three walks of 10 minutes. The chair stands become sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, two to three sets. Balance gets harder: tandem with light support, side steps along the worktop, then standing on one foot. If a professional allows it, add ankle weights of about 1 kg, the starting load of the Otago programmes.19 Criterion to move up: you have done at least 2 sessions out of 3 for four weeks, without pain lasting more than one to two days and without dizziness (editorial proposal).

Weeks 9 to 12: consolidate and repeat the measurements (about 135 minutes a week)

Three sessions of 30 minutes, three walks of 15 minutes. In week 12, repeat the three measurements under the same conditions (same chair, same shoes, same time of day). Read the result with caution: a single SPPB point of difference may be noise, the standard error of measurement of the battery being 1.42 points; the change judged substantial is 1.34 points.17 You therefore need a clear difference or several concordant measurements. A retest at week 6 is possible, as a guide.

Afterwards: maintain (about 150 minutes a week)

Three sessions of 30 minutes, two outings of 30 minutes. This is the dose of the Otago programme. Repeat the measurements every 3 to 6 months; this frequency is an editorial recommendation, without a source (the LIFE trial checked its participants every 6 months).18 In LIFE (1,635 people aged 70 to 89, sedentary, SPPB of 9 or less), a structured programme of walking, strengthening, balance and flexibility reduced the loss of the ability to walk 400 metres (risk ratio of 0.82 over 2.6 years). Serious adverse events were slightly more frequent in the active group (49.4% against 45.7%), though the difference was not established.18 The effect is moderate, and caution remains appropriate.

Move forward, stay, step back

Move forward when you have kept to the rhythm for four weeks, with no lasting pain and no dizziness.

Stay in the same phase if you have missed more than one session in three or if you are tired: repeat an identical week. A missed day is not serious (Lally).25

Step back one phase after an illness, an interruption of more than one to two weeks, or pain lasting more than one or two days after exercise (the AAFP threshold for talking to a doctor).24 Stepping back does not mean failing: the programmes studied also progress in stages.

Common mistakes, warning signs, when to stop

Common mistakes (editorial reading): doing only walking; waiting until you are no longer afraid before starting; skipping balance because it is uncomfortable; progressing too fast after a good start; giving up everything after one missed week; testing yourself every day, which only shows noise.

Stop the session and contact a doctor if you have
  • pain or pressure in the chest, or difficulty breathing;
  • a sudden cold sweat;
  • a feeling of light-headedness, dizziness or nausea;
  • severe joint pain or severe cramps.24

Also talk to a doctor if pain lasts more than one or two days after exercise.24 After a fall, a consultation is recommended by the HAS.22 Suspend the programme until you have advice: a fall, a new symptom, a change in treatment, an acute illness.

The frank answer

Solid. Exercise programmes that work on balance reduce falls in older people living at home, with high certainty (Cochrane, 108 trials). The muscles of frail people aged 87 to 90 respond to strength training (Fiatarone, randomised trial of 100 people). Exercise does not increase falls (Cochrane on the fear of falling).

Probable. A programme combining strength, balance and walking gives more consistent results in frail people (Cadore: in the majority of trials, not all); a structured programme delays the loss of the ability to walk (one trial, LIFE); group exercise works better than one-to-one for frailty (one review, effects not quantified in the part read).

Proposal, not demonstrated. The doses by phase, the criteria for moving forward or back, the retest frequencies, an individual's protein dose, help for those close to them. The trials show the effect of a programme on groups: that improving a score reduces your own risk is not proven.

The practical answer: yes, it is worth it, provided you start small, with a doctor's advice, strengthening the legs, working on balance, measuring, and repeating it. It is neither simple nor insurmountable: the difficulty is not knowing what to do, it is doing it again tomorrow.

Limitations
  • Many trials concern nursing-home residents or hospitalised patients, volunteers, in a supervised setting: your results at home may differ.
  • The summary read of the Cochrane review on falls says nothing about frail people or nursing homes.
  • Lally's study concerns students, not older people.
  • The doses and progression criteria in the “action plan” section are proposals, with no trial of this trajectory.

Frequently asked questions

I am close to a frail older person: should I push them?

Suggest rather than impose. Help them ask for the doctor's advice, prepare a safe place, choose a group session. The HAS speaks of negotiating, with their fears and their values.22

I have already fallen: should I stop moving?

First have a consultation after the fall, that is the HAS recommendation. After that, exercise did not increase falls in the trials, and balance programmes reduce them.22,13,12

Should I take protein supplements?

The question depends on your kidneys, your illnesses and your diet: it is one for your doctor or a dietitian. The PROT-AGE recommendations aim for 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/day at minimum, but the supplement alone did not improve strength in the 1994 Fiatarone trial.20,6
